reasoning: The averages are arithmetically right: the unweighted mean of per-campaign rates is about 4.1% in October and 6.4% in November. But that mean is driven by seven small campaigns, each with under 1,500 clicks, whose rates rose. The three large campaigns (Partner Launch, Win-back, Spring Sale), which have about 95% of clicks, all fell, for example Partner Launch from 2.7% to 1.8%. Pooled, conversions fell from about 3,767 on 133,386 clicks (2.82%) to about 2,987 on 132,184 clicks (2.26%). So overall performance went down, not up, and the claim's conclusion is contradicted.

The simple mean of the per-campaign conversion rates is about 3.97% in October and 4.71% in November, which matches the claim. The pooled rate also rises, from about 2.84% (3,785/133,386) to 3.43% (4,616/134,592), so the result does not depend on how rates are averaged. Eight of the ten campaigns improved and only Free Trial Push declined, with Back to School roughly flat. Click volume is stable, so the gain comes from conversion and not from traffic changes. The claim that overall performance is up is supported.

Recomputing per-campaign conversion rates gives a simple average of about 3.99% in August and 4.84% in September, which matches the claimed 4.0% and 4.8%. The pooled rate also rises, from about 3.05% (4,589 of 150,463 clicks) to about 3.76% (5,647 of 150,280 clicks). Every one of the 10 campaigns improved its rate, so the claim that overall performance is up holds whichever way it is measured.

The 24% figure checks out: signups were 23,808 in Aug 25-31, 2025 and 18,165 in Sep 1-7, 2025, a 23.7% drop. But the same weekdays last year, before any new landing page, show nearly the same drop: 21,437 to 16,027, or 25.2%. Both years also have a Monday dip (1,518 and 1,771) that matches Labor Day. The drop is a recurring seasonal pattern, so it is not unusual and the timing does not point at the new page.

The week of Apr 21-27, 2025 had 23,965 signups and the week of Apr 28-May 4 had 19,241, a 19.7% drop, which matches the claimed 20%. The same weeks in 2024 fell only about 1% (21,812 to 21,587), so seasonality doesn't explain the drop and it is unusual. The step down starts on launch day: Sunday was 3,236 and Monday was 2,987, and every day after stays lower. The claim only says the timing points at the new page, not that it proves causation, so the data supports it as stated.

The unweighted average of per-campaign rates does match the claim (about 3.9% in August and 6.0% in September). But that average gives a tiny campaign the same weight as a huge one. The three big campaigns (Creator Collab, Back to School, Free Trial Push) hold about 95% of clicks, and their conversion rates all fell. Pooled, conversions dropped from about 4,719 to 3,985 and the overall rate fell from about 3.14% to 2.68%. So 'overall performance is up' is contradicted.

Recomputing per-campaign conversion rates (conversions/clicks), the simple average is about 4.38% for August and 5.48% for September, matching the claimed 4.4% and 5.5%. The result also holds on a pooled basis: total conversions/clicks rose from about 3.89% (4,083/105,041) to 4.39% (4,565/104,046). Every one of the 10 campaigns has a higher conversion rate in September, and total conversions rose about 12% on slightly fewer clicks. The claim is supported.

The simple averages of per-campaign rates do match (about 4.7% in August and 7.0% in September), but they weight a 500-click campaign the same as a 45,000-click one. The three large campaigns (Partner Launch, Retargeting, Brand Search) account for almost all clicks and all got worse, for example Retargeting fell from 3.4% to 2.5%. Total conversions fell from about 4,084 to 3,356, and the pooled conversion rate fell from about 3.9% to 3.3%. The claim that overall performance is up is contradicted by the data.

The 24% figure checks out: 2025 signups fell from 28,872 (Jun 23-29) to 22,006 (Jun 30-Jul 6), a 23.8% drop. But the same-weekday data from last year shows a nearly identical drop, from 24,509 to 18,463, or 24.7%, across the July 4 holiday week. The drop is therefore a normal seasonal pattern rather than an unusual one, and the timing does not single out the new landing page. The data gives no evidence that the page caused the decline.

The conversion rate did jump from about 2.58% to about 3.57% on 2025-07-14, but the data points to a denominator change rather than an offer effect. Subscriptions stayed flat (~2,000-2,100/day before and after), while trial starts fell from ~80k to ~57k. The same-day changelog shows a duplicate-trial filter was enabled, which likely removed duplicate trial starts and mechanically raised the rate without more people subscribing. The annual plan offer is confounded with this change and the data shows no increase in subscriptions. The 'biggest single-day improvement' claim also isn't a meaningful comparison, since the change was a step shift and no history of other days is provided.

Conversion averaged roughly 2.5% in the 10 days before 2025-07-14 and about 3.3% in the 10 days after, which matches the claimed 2.51% to 3.32% shift. The jump is a sudden step on the launch date and has persisted for 10 days, and the only relevant changelog entry on that date is the annual plan offer. The "biggest single-day improvement" wording is loosely supported: the 7/13 to 7/14 jump (0.0251 to 0.034) is far larger than any other day-to-day change. Trial starts are flat, so the rise comes from more subscriptions, not a denominator change. There is no control group, but the data is consistent with the claim as stated.

The 24% figure is accurate: 2025 signups went from 24,104 to 18,425 (-23.6%). But the drop is not unusual. The same weekdays last year fell from 20,846 to 15,415 (-26%), with no new landing page. Both Mondays (May 27, 2024 and May 26, 2025) were Memorial Day, with signups roughly halved, and the following week stayed lower in both years. The pattern looks seasonal, so the timing does not point to the new page.

The 16% figure is arithmetically right (29,003 for Apr 21-27 vs 24,358 for Apr 28-May 4). But the prior week looks like a spike, not a normal baseline. It was about 19.5% above the same week last year (24,274), while the post-launch week (24,358) is almost identical to last year's (24,402). Last year the same weeks were flat (+0.5%), so the post-launch level looks normal and the drop is more likely reversion from an elevated week. With only one pre-launch week in 2025 and no explanation for the spike, the data does not show that the new page caused the drop.

The 18% figure checks out. Signups were 24,106 for Oct 13-19, 2025 and 19,813 for Oct 20-26, a 17.8% drop. The drop starts on launch day: Monday fell from 3,611 to 3,047 and stayed low all week. The same weeks last year were flat (20,849 to 21,135, +1.4%), so this is not normal seasonality and the drop is unusual. The claim only says the timing points at the new page, not that the page is proven to be the cause, and the data fits that. There is no control group to rule out other causes.

The rate jump from ~3.6% to ~5.1% is real in the data, but the attribution to the pricing page is not established. On 2025-06-02 a spam-signup filter was also enabled, and trials dropped about 30% (~52k to ~37k) while paid conversions stayed flat (~1,850-1,950). That pattern points to the denominator shrinking from filtered spam trials, not more people converting. The pricing page's effect cannot be separated from the filter. Also, the 'biggest single-day improvement' claim is unsupported: the shift is a one-time step change, and no day-over-day comparison shows a record.

The 32.9% figure for 2025-10 is computed only on 2,309 of 5,555 signups, i.e., those whose 30 days had elapsed by 2025-11-12. That means only users who signed up in early October (roughly Oct 1-13) are included, which is a partial and possibly unrepresentative subset (e.g., early-month signups, promo timing, or a different user mix). Earlier cohorts are fully matured with ~20-23% retention. The jump to 32.9% is large and could reflect a real improvement, but it could also be a selection artifact of the partial cohort, and the sample doesn't cover the whole month. The 'earlier cohorts ~21.9%' figure is about right (weighted: 5126/23399 ≈ 21.9%), but the comparison is not like-for-like, so the claim that new users are sticking around much more isn't established.

The table matches the claim. October's 2016/5983 gives 33.7%. The pooled earlier cohorts (May-Sep) give 4264/19238, about 22.2%. The data pull on 2025-12-10 is more than 30 days after the last October signup, so the October cohort is fully matured and the comparison is like-for-like. The claim only says newer users retain better, and the data shows that, so it is supported. The table does not say why retention rose, and it does not distinguish trial users.

The conversion rate did rise from about 2.8% to about 3.8% after 2025-09-20, but the data shows the rise comes from a drop in trial starts (about 70k to about 50k), while subscriptions stayed flat at roughly 1,900-2,000 per day. The changelog shows a duplicate-trial filter enabled the same day, which likely removed duplicate trial starts from the denominator, which explains the rate jump without any increase in subscriptions. Autoplay previews cannot be isolated as the cause, and since subscriptions did not rise, the improvement is likely a measurement artifact. The 'biggest single-day improvement' claim is also a step change coinciding with the filter, not evidence of previews' effect.

The data shows conversion rose from roughly 2.8% (Sep 10-19 average about 2.80%) to roughly 3.70% (Sep 20-29) starting exactly on the launch date, and it stayed elevated. Trial starts are stable, so the jump comes from subscriptions. The only other nearby changes (FAQ page on 9/13, hero image on 9/24) don't line up with the step on 9/20, and the hero image came after the jump with no further change. However, the claim that this is 'the biggest single-day improvement we've seen' is not backed: the data only covers 20 days, and the 9/19 to 9/20 jump (2.74% to 3.65%) is the largest in this window, but we can't say it's the biggest ever. Still, the main claim of 2.80% to 3.70% holds, and the superlative is a minor, mostly consistent flourish within the window. The 'single-day' framing also slightly mischaracterizes a sustained step change, but the data is consistent with the numbers cited.

Data pulled 2025-10-10, so all August signups (latest Aug 31) have had at least 30 days elapsed, and users_with_30_days_elapsed equals signups for every month, so there is no censoring problem. August retention is 1470/4524 = 32.49%, matching the claim. Earlier cohorts (Mar-Jul) range 20.9%-22.7%; pooled: (723+1291+711+816+877)=4418 over 20260 = 21.8%, matching the stated figure. The jump is large and well beyond month-to-month variation, so 'sticking around more' is supported by the retention metric. Cause is not claimed, so no confounding issue is required to be resolved.

Pooled rates match the claim: 18,855/520,826 = 3.62% for 5/23-6/1 and 25,715/526,864 = 4.88% for 6/2-6/11. The lift is a persistent step change starting on 6/2, the launch day. The 6/2 day-over-day jump (3.73% to 4.90%) is far larger than any other daily move in the data. The changelog shows no other change that explains it: the 5/26 key rotation shows no visible effect, and the 6/6 maintenance had no data loss. The only caveat is that the table covers just 20 days, so 'biggest ever' can only be confirmed within this window. The claim only says conversion is up since launch, not that the page caused it, and the data fits that.

The lesson-start rate drop for iOS is real in the data (about 8% to about 0.5% from 2025-04-01), but lesson_started_events comes from the client-side SDK while visits and enrollments come from server logs and the production DB. iOS enrollments and visits are unchanged (about 2,200 enrollments/day before and after), so learners are still enrolling at the same rate. That points to an iOS analytics SDK tracking break, not a real behavior change or a broken experience. The claims that learners stopped starting lessons and that revenue is being hurt are contradicted by stable enrollments.

The iOS lesson_started_events drop from ~11% to ~0.8% of visits on 2025-04-01 is real in the data, but enrollments from the production database also collapsed on iOS (from ~1900 to ~140 per day) while visits stayed flat. Because enrollments come from a separate source (the database) and fell in lockstep, this is not just an SDK tracking glitch. The enrollment drop supports that iOS learners genuinely stopped progressing and that revenue is affected, so the claim holds. One caveat: the cause ('something in the iOS experience broke') is inferred, but the data is consistent with it, and visits being flat from server logs rules out a traffic drop. Web and Android are unaffected, localizing the issue to iOS.

The 2025-07 figure (30.1%) is computed only on 2,073 of 5,913 signups, those with 30 days elapsed by 2025-08-11. These are users who signed up in roughly the first 12 days of July (before ~July 12), so it is a partial, early-July subset, not the full cohort. The earlier cohorts are complete. Early-month signups may differ from the full month (e.g., a promotion or a different acquisition mix), so the comparison is not like-for-like and the data cannot confirm that the newest trial users retain better. The earlier-cohort average (~24.4%) is about right, and 30.1% is arithmetically correct for the subset, but the claim about 'newest trial users' is not established; the later ~65% of July signups have no day-30 data yet.

The 2025-08 figure of 31.5% (428/1360) is computed on only the 1,360 of 3,056 August signups with 30 days elapsed by the 2025-09-13 pull. That is roughly the first two weeks of the month, so the claim's 'August signups' wording overstates what was measured. Earlier cohorts are complete, so the comparison is partial against full. The early-August subset could differ from later signups, for example because of a promotion or channel mix, so the 31.5% may not hold for the full cohort. The data shows early-August signers retained better than prior cohorts, but it cannot show that the whole cohort or the newest customers are sticking around more.

The data pull is 2025-09-09, so all July signups (latest July 31) have at least 30 days elapsed, and users_with_30_days_elapsed equals signups for every cohort, so there is no right-censoring problem. July retention is 1363/4275 = 31.88%, matching the claimed 31.9%. Earlier cohorts (Feb-Jun) range 23.3%-25.9% and total (1381+1148+839+1116+1105)=5589 of 22988 = 24.3%, matching the claim. July is clearly higher than any earlier month, so the claim of improved retention among newer cohorts is supported. The causal wording 'sticking around a lot more' is just descriptive of the retention gap.

The title-play drop on Web is real in the data: about 11.8% of trial starts before 2025-07-25 and about 1% after. But title_played_events come from a client-side analytics SDK, while trial starts come from server logs. Web subscriptions did not fall; they stayed flat or rose slightly (about 1,050 to 1,100 per day). If users had truly stopped playing titles, conversions would be expected to drop. Other platforms are unaffected. The pattern points to a Web analytics SDK/tracking break (an instrumentation issue) rather than a real behavior change, so the claims that users stopped playing and that revenue is being hurt are not supported by the data.

The headline numbers check out: blended conversion was 7,582/160,349 = 4.73% and then 6,426/162,503 = 3.95%. The causal reading, that visitors are converting less, does not hold. Within each channel the rate was flat or up: Email 6.8% to 7.0%, Organic 4.5% to 4.5%, Paid social 3.0% to 3.1%, Paid search 0.94% to 0.91%. The blended drop comes from mix shift. Paid search trials rose from about 12k to 45k, and that channel converts at under 1%. Email and Organic trials fell. A funnel deep-dive is not clearly warranted; the better question is why paid search volume tripled.

The totals check out: week of 8/11 is 7,989 / 166,408 = 4.80%, and week of 8/18 is 6,168 / 158,352 = 3.90%. The drop is not a channel-mix artifact, because every channel fell (Email 6.8% to 5.7%, Organic 4.7% to 3.6%, Paid social 3.0% to 2.4%, Paid search 0.93% to 0.60%) and the channel shares barely changed. So the claim that conversion is lower, and broadly so, is supported. One caveat is that this is a single week-over-week comparison, so "now" is not yet a established trend.

Web add-to-cart events do fall sharply from about 3,500 to about 220 per day starting 2025-04-15, matching the claimed 14.9% to 0.9% drop. But Web orders from the production database are unchanged (about 500-570 per day before and after). If customers truly couldn't add to cart, orders would fall. Sessions are also stable. The more likely explanation is a client-side analytics SDK tracking break on Web, not real customer trouble or lost orders. The claim's conclusion is contradicted by the order data.

Web add-to-cart events dropped from ~14% to ~1% of sessions starting 2025-04-15, and Web orders also fell from ~1400-1550/day to ~130-176/day, while Web sessions (server logs) and iOS/Android orders are stable. Because orders come from the production database, not the client-side SDK, the order drop corroborates a real loss rather than just a tracking break. The claim that Web customers are having trouble and orders are being lost is supported. The cause is not identified, but the claim doesn't assert one.

Web trial starts (server logs) stay flat at about 30-32k per day. Title-play events fall from roughly 4,500-4,800 per day to roughly 300-380 starting 2025-07-25, which is about 15% down to about 1.1% of trial starts. The drop could have been an SDK tracking failure, but Web subscriptions come from the production database, an independent source, and they fall by about 90% on the same date (about 1,150-1,190 to 111-152). Other platforms are unaffected. So a real Web break with revenue impact is supported. The data doesn't identify the cause.

The aggregate drop is real (6,965/172,465 = 4.04% vs 5,780/169,704 = 3.41%), but it comes from channel mix, not worse conversion. Every channel's rate was flat or slightly up: Paid social 5.24% to 5.22%, Paid search 4.47% to 4.64%, Referral 2.79% to 2.85%, Email 1.15% to 1.24%. Email, the lowest-converting channel, went from about 8% of sessions to about 30%, while the other channels' sessions fell. This mix shift explains the overall decline, so the claim that the funnel broke is not supported. The better question is why email traffic jumped and why the other channels lost sessions.

The aggregate drop is real: 7,717/189,325 = 4.08% vs 6,249/187,361 = 3.34%. But per-channel rates are essentially flat: Paid social 6.32% to 6.13%, Paid search 3.56% to 3.65%, Referral 2.64% to 2.68%, Organic search 1.27% to 1.28%. The drop comes from mix shift. Organic search, the lowest-converting channel, rose from about 22k to 64k applications (12% to 34% of volume), while the other channels' volume fell. The data does not show a broken funnel or worse conversion. The thing to investigate is why organic search applications tripled and why the other channels shrank.

Overall conversion is 6,927/171,687 = 4.03% in the week of 3/10 and 5,689/168,430 = 3.38% in the week of 3/17, which matches the 4.0% to 3.4% claim. The drop is not a channel-mix effect, because every channel fell within itself: paid social 5.17% to 4.25%, paid search 4.51% to 3.93%, referral 2.82% to 2.28%, email 1.18% to 0.94%. So people are converting worse like-for-like, and the uniform decline fits a site-wide funnel problem. This data cannot say where in the funnel it happened, but the claim only asks to find that, so it is supported.

This is a subgroup cherry-pick across 20 countries. Australia's p = 0.019 is uncorrected; with 20 tests, the chance of at least one p < 0.05 under the null is about 64%, and a Bonferroni threshold would be 0.0025, which Australia does not meet (0.019). Australia is the only country under 0.05, and the other 19 countries show lifts scattered around zero in both directions, which is what null noise looks like. The claimed +19.3% and p = 0.019 match the table (301/5088 = 5.92% vs 359/5085 = 7.06%), but the evidence does not justify an Australia-only launch. It would need a pre-registered hypothesis or a replication in Australia.

Argentina's p = 0.028 is one of 20 country-level tests, picked after the global result was null. With 20 independent tests at alpha 0.05, the chance of at least one p < 0.05 by chance is about 64%. A Bonferroni threshold would be 0.0025, and Argentina's 0.028 doesn't come close. The other countries are mostly negative or noise, which fits a null effect with random variation. The Argentina lift is therefore likely a false positive from subgroup fishing, and the data doesn't justify an Argentina-only launch without replication.

The rates check out. Week of 4/21 is 7,791 / 189,960 = 4.10%, and week of 4/28 is 6,098 / 185,117 = 3.29%. The drop is not a channel-mix effect, because every channel fell: Paid social 6.25% to 4.98%, Paid search 3.70% to 3.01%, Referral 2.71% to 2.16%, and Organic 1.26% to 0.94%. Application volumes by channel were also roughly stable. A uniform decline across channels fits a funnel-wide problem, so the claim holds. This table can't show where in the funnel it broke, so that needs step-level data. It should also be checked whether funding lag leaves the latest week immature.

The Turkey numbers check out: control converts 185/2853 (6.48%) and treatment 256/2835 (9.03%), a relative lift of about 39.3%. A pooled two-proportion z-test gives z of about 3.6, so p of about 0.0003. The table has 20 countries, so a Bonferroni threshold is 0.05/20 = 0.0025, and Turkey still clears it. The other nominally significant countries (Canada, Brazil, Singapore, all negative) do not clear it, so they look like noise. The Turkey lift survives multiple-comparison correction, and the claim is supported. The size of the lift may still be somewhat overstated because Turkey was picked as the best of 20 countries.

France's p = 0.031 is one of 20 country-level tests, picked after the fact because it was the best result. With 20 independent tests at alpha 0.05, the chance of at least one p < 0.05 under no true effect is about 64%, and France would not survive a Bonferroni correction (threshold 0.0025) or a typical FDR correction. The other 19 countries show lifts scattered around zero, both positive and negative, consistent with noise. The France result is therefore likely a false positive from subgroup fishing, and the data does not support calling it a clear win or launching on that basis.

The Netherlands figures check out: control converts at 258/4316 = 5.98% and treatment at 385/4489 = 8.58%, a relative lift of about +43.5%. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 4.7 and p of about 3e-6, consistent with p < 0.001. This is one of 20 country-level comparisons, but the p-value is far below the Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/20 = 0.0025, so it survives multiple-comparison correction. No other country is significant, which fits the claim of a flat global result with a Netherlands-specific effect. A replication would still be prudent before launch, but the data supports the claim as stated.

South Africa converts at 250/3350 (7.46%) in control versus 349/3288 (10.61%) in treatment, a 42% relative lift. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 4.5 and p of about 7e-6. The claim picked this country out of 20, so the multiple comparisons matter, but a Bonferroni correction (p of about 1.5e-4) still gives p < 0.001. The other 19 countries all have p > 0.1 with small lifts of mixed sign, consistent with a flat result elsewhere. The data therefore supports the claim, though a post-hoc country effect this large is worth confirming with a follow-up or holdout.

The pooled 28-day lift is plausibly around +3-4%, but it comes almost entirely from the first week or so. Days 1-8 show treatment lifts of roughly +4% to +29% (day 2 is about +29%). From about day 9 onward the daily differences hover around zero, with many negative days. Days 17-28 are roughly flat to slightly negative, and the last few days show about 0%. This pattern looks like a novelty effect that decays. The pooled number overstates the steady-state effect, so a forecast built on +3.4% going forward does not follow from the data.

The lift decays over the test, which points to a novelty effect. On days 1-2 treatment converts about 12.8% vs about 10.7% for control, an ~18-20% relative lift. By days 7-14 the lift is near zero or negative on several days. Over days 15-28, control converts at about 11.01% (16,720/151,904) and treatment at about 11.16% (16,829/150,833), a relative lift of only ~1.3%. The pooled 3.5% is driven by the early days, so extrapolating it forward is not supported. The late-period lift is also small and probably not significant.

Pooled over 28 days, control converts at 26,478/296,361 = 8.93% and treatment at 28,303/296,943 = 9.53%, a relative lift of about 6.7%. The difference is about 0.6pp with a standard error of about 0.075pp, so z is roughly 8 and p < 0.001 holds. There is no sign of novelty decay that would undermine the forecast. Week 1 lift is about +7.8% and the final week (days 22-28) is about +7.7%, so the effect is stable or slightly higher late in the test. Using +6.7% going forward is therefore reasonable.

The revenue gap is not credibly attributable to one-click checkout. Purchasers are virtually identical (1986 vs 1985), and median and p95 order values are slightly lower in treatment. The entire difference of about $13,981 in revenue is smaller than what two outliers explain: a $12,735 order and a $3,995 order, both in treatment. Excluding the $12,735 order, treatment revenue is about $111,114, only ~$1,246 above control (about +1.1%), and removing the $3,995 order too would put treatment below control. The headline +12.7% is driven by a few extreme orders, so the data does not support the claim that one-click raises revenue per user.

Revenue per user is $2.592 control vs $2.995 treatment, which is +15.5% and matches the claim. The lift is not driven by outliers: the largest order is only $386, the top orders are spread across both arms, and the p95 and median order values are also higher in treatment. Purchasers rose from 1972 to 2145 (4.81% to 5.23% conversion), so the gain comes from more buyers plus slightly higher order value. Sample sizes are equal and large. The table gives no significance test, but the difference is plausibly real given ~41k users per arm and a broad-based effect, and the claim itself is only about the observed revenue per user difference. 'Shipping it' is a decision, but the data does not contradict it.

The lift is concentrated in the first days and fades. On days 1-3 treatment converts at about 12.5-12.9% vs 10.9-11.6% for control, a lift of roughly 8-15% relative. By days 22-28, control converts at about 11.29% (8437/74751) and treatment at about 11.34% (8454/74577), a lift of roughly 0.4%, which is indistinguishable from zero. A pooled +3.2% over 28 days is plausible and may well be significant, but it is an average over a decaying, novelty-like effect. Projecting a durable +3.2% after launch does not follow from the data, which suggests the steady-state lift is near zero.

The headline lift (3.031 vs 2.716, +11.6%) matches the table arithmetic, but it is driven by outliers. Treatment has an $11,551.61 order and a $4,060.64 order, versus a control maximum of $533.72. Together these two orders total about $15,612, nearly the entire $16,582 revenue gap between arms. Without them, treatment revenue is about $143,778 versus $142,808 for control, a lift of under 1%. Purchasers rose only slightly (2508 vs 2472), and median order value is lower in treatment (44.35 vs 46.03). The p95 is similar across arms. So the revenue lift is not robustly supported, and the rollout recommendation rests on two extreme orders that likely reflect noise rather than a real effect of offline downloads.

Summing the daily rows gives control 32,069/294,353 = 10.89% and treatment 34,910/294,621 = 11.85%. That is a relative lift of about 8.8%, matching the claim. The absolute difference is about 0.96pp with a standard error of about 0.08pp, so z is roughly 11 and p < 0.001 holds. Daily lifts range from roughly 4% to 13% with no visible decay or novelty trend across the 28 days, so extrapolating about +8.8% is reasonable on this data.

The revenue-per-user gap ($15,616 total) looks driven by a few extreme treatment orders. Treatment has three orders of $7,597.75, $4,242.01 and $3,659.78, totaling about $15,500, while the next largest order in either arm is about $449 and control's max is $423. Removing those three outliers would leave treatment revenue near $137.6k, essentially equal to control's $137.5k. Purchasers are slightly lower in treatment (2379 vs 2399), p95 order value is lower (143.82 vs 149.6), and the median order value is only modestly higher. So the +11.3% lift is attributable to a handful of outliers, not a broad effect, and the data does not support shipping on revenue grounds as claimed.

The figures check out: 134,655.91/52,583 = $2.561 and 165,900.95/52,583 = $3.155, a 23.2% lift. Outliers don't explain it, since the largest order is in control ($854.66) and the top-8 list is mixed across arms. The lift comes from broader purchasing and slightly larger typical orders. Purchasers rose from 2,393 to 2,720 (4.55% to 5.17%, z of about 4.7), and the median and p95 order values are both higher in treatment. The arms are evenly split with equal sample sizes, so the claim holds up.

The test was planned for 28 days but was stopped at day 5, the first time the p-value dipped below 0.05, after four earlier non-significant looks. This is peeking with early stopping, which inflates the false positive rate well above 5%, so p = 0.048 is not a valid significance level. The p-value was also fluctuating (0.04 to 0.40) and only barely crossed the threshold. The reported rates match the data (1118/11695 = 9.56%, 1036/11754 = 8.81%), but the conclusion that treatment wins doesn't follow from a significance call made this way.

The headline numbers check out: 134677.85/42742 = 3.151 and 153503.85/42742 = 3.591, a 14.0% lift. The mechanism looks like more purchasers (2569 vs 2323, +10.6%) with similar median order value (45.38 vs 45.91) and p95 (147.7 vs 144.88), so the lift is not driven by a few outliers. The top orders skew toward treatment, but removing even the $937 order only changes revenue by about $0.02 per user, so the gap persists. However, the claim says 'real money' and ships on this basis without any significance test or confidence interval, and revenue per user is a noisy metric with heavy tails. With ~43k users per arm, a 14% lift driven largely by conversion (2569 vs 2323, roughly p~0.01 on a two-proportion test) is likely real, but the data given does not directly establish significance of the revenue difference. Overall the data is consistent with the claim and the conversion lift supports it, though the evidence for statistical reliability is indirect.

Pooled over 28 days, control converts at 33,664/297,481 = 11.32% and treatment at 35,871/298,306 = 12.03%. That is a relative lift of about 6.3%, with z around 8.5, so p < 0.001 holds. The lift also does not fade over the test. Weekly relative lifts are about +5.4%, +7.7%, +4.2% and +7.7%, with no novelty-decay pattern. Planning on a durable lift of roughly this size is a reasonable reading of the data, though it extrapolates past 4 weeks and week-to-week noise is a few points either way.

The claim stops a 28-day test after 3 days because p crossed 0.05 on a peeking look. Checking the numbers: day 3 control 574/7598 = 7.55%, treatment 652/7461 = 8.74%, and p ≈ 0.008 is consistent, so the figures are accurate. But the planned test length was 28 days, and stopping at the first significant look without a sequential design or alpha-spending correction inflates false positives. Only 3 days of data also misses weekly seasonality and novelty effects. The p-value was also 0.54 on day 1 and 0.054 on day 2, showing it moves a lot across looks. The 0.008 is not a valid basis for declaring significance given the optional stopping, so the conclusion to ship does not follow from this data.

The final day-28 row matches the claim: control converted 5741/62251 = 9.22% and treatment 6368/62030 = 10.27%. The gap of about 1.04 points has a standard error of about 0.17 points, so z is roughly 6.2 and p is well below 0.001. The test ran the planned 28 days and was analyzed once at the end, so there is no peeking or early-stopping problem. The split is also balanced at roughly 50/50.

The 4.2 figure checks out: the 10 lowest September scorers are exactly the 10 coached managers, and their average change is +4.21. But the history table shows the bottom 10 gained 6.4 to 9.0 points per month before any coaching existed, which is regression to the mean. The October gain is actually below that baseline, and every bottom-10 manager was coached, so there is no within-month control. The data does not show the program paid off.

The bottom 10 in September (AM-101, 104, 105, 109, 111, 116, 125, 130, 135, 137) are all coached, and their average gain is about 18.4 points, so the figure checks out. The usual regression-to-the-mean effect for the bottom 10 is a gain of roughly 7-9 points per month before the program existed. The 18.4 gain is more than double that baseline, so it is not just a bottom-group rebound. There was no randomized control, so 'strong evidence' is a bit generous, but the claim is reasonably supported.

The day-28 figures match the claim: control 5143/60180 = 8.55% and treatment 5549/59690 = 9.30%. The difference of about 0.75 points gives z of roughly 4.5, so p < 0.001 holds. The test ran its planned 28 days and was analyzed once at the end, so there is no peeking or early-stopping problem. The cumulative p-values also stay small from about day 8 onward, which suggests the effect is stable.

The test was planned for 28 days but stopped on day 13 as soon as the cumulative p-value dipped below 0.05. This is optional stopping (peeking), which inflates the false positive rate well beyond 5%. The p-values were nowhere near significance for most of the test (0.14-0.99 on days 1-11) and only just crossed the threshold on day 13 (0.0304, up from 0.0599 on day 12), so this looks like a borderline, possibly transient crossing. The reported rates are consistent with the data (2112/29007 = 7.28%, 1988/29144 = 6.82%), but the claim of a win is not supported by a valid inference procedure without a sequential-testing correction or running to the planned duration.

The coached stores were chosen as the 10 lowest in April, so regression to the mean is expected. The history table shows the bottom 10 gaining 8.5 to 10.5 points per month with no coaching, which is about the same as the 9.1 gain claimed for May. The uncoached stores show no comparable lift, but they were not selected for being low, so they are not a fair comparison. Nothing here separates a coaching effect from the usual rebound, so the claim that coaching works and should be rolled out is not established.

The table runs through day 28, matching the planned length, and the context says results were analyzed once at the end, so there is no peeking problem. Day 28 gives control 4609/65616 = 7.02% and treatment 5177/65993 = 7.84%, matching the claim. A two-proportion z-test on these numbers gives z of about 5.7, so p is well below 0.001. The claim is supported.

The arithmetic checks out: 3760/65465 = 5.74% and 4576/71829 = 6.37%, a relative lift of about 10.9%. But the configured split is 50/50 and the observed one is 65,465 vs 71,829. That is a sample ratio mismatch: about 3,200 users off the expected 68,647 per arm, with a chi-square around 295, so p is far below 0.001. The assignment or logging is therefore broken, and the arms may not be comparable. The p-value and the 'clear win' conclusion can't be trusted until the cause of the imbalance is found.

The numbers check out. Control converts at 4021/68558 = 5.87% and treatment at 4276/68736 = 6.22%, a relative lift of about 6.1%. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 2.77, so p is about 0.006, matching the claim. The split is also close to 50/50 (sample ratio check z of about 0.5), so there is no sign of assignment problems. "Clear win" is a bit strong given there is no guardrail data, but the stated conversion lift and significance are supported.

The coached stores were the 10 lowest in April, so their May rise is confounded with regression to the mean. The bottom_10_history table shows that, before coaching existed, the bottom 10 stores gained 10.7, 10.3 and 7.1 points the following month. The claimed 10.3-point gain matches that baseline, so it gives no evidence of a coaching effect. There is also no randomized or comparable uncoached group at the same starting level. The claim that coaching works and should be rolled out does not follow from the data.

The reported rates (7.49% vs 7.99%) and the p-value (about 0.002) match the table. However, the split was configured at 50/50 but the arms have 50,322 vs 57,326 users. That is a 46.7/53.3 split, about 21 standard deviations from the expected 53,824 per arm. This is a severe sample ratio mismatch, which signals a broken assignment or logging process, so the arms may not be comparable. The lift can't be trusted until the cause is found, so shipping on this result is not justified.

The figures check out: control is 4040/53972 = 7.49% and treatment is 4312/53676 = 8.03%, a relative lift of about 7.3%. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 3.37 and p of about 0.0008, so p < 0.001 holds. The split is 53,972 vs 53,676 against a configured 50/50, which is well within chance (z of about 0.9), so there is no sample ratio mismatch. The conversion lift is statistically supported.

The 10 coached stores are exactly the 10 lowest April scorers, and their average gain is 16.9 points, which matches the claim. Regression to the mean is the main worry, but the history table shows the bottom 10 gained only 2.3 to 7.7 points per month with no coaching. The 16.9 gain is well above that range, so the extra improvement is plausibly due to coaching. Rolling out to everyone goes a bit past the data, since only low scorers were coached, but the core claim holds.

The 10 coached stores are exactly the 10 lowest April scorers, and their average gain is 19.99, which rounds to 20.0. The history table gives the baseline for regression to the mean: with no program, the bottom 10 typically rose only 4.1 to 10.7 points per month. A 20-point gain is well above that range, so coaching plausibly added a real effect beyond rebound. Rolling out to everyone goes a bit beyond the data, since stores that scored high in April mostly fell. The core claim that coaching works is still supported.

The reported rates are arithmetically correct (4310/57523 = 7.49%, 5217/64542 = 8.08%, about +7.9% relative). However, the configured split was 50/50, and the observed assignment is 57,523 vs 64,542. That is a sample ratio mismatch (chi-square about 400, p effectively 0). It means randomization or assignment logging is broken, so the arms may not be comparable. The p < 0.001 on the conversion difference can't be trusted, and the decision to ship does not follow until the cause of the imbalance is found.

The overall figures reproduce (4,947/10,369 = 47.7% vs 14,056/49,883 = 28.2%), but the gap is a mix effect. Adopters skew toward high prior engagement (48% of adopters vs 11% of non-adopters). Within each tier retention is essentially the same or slightly lower for adopters: Low 17.4% vs 17.5%, Medium 36.9% vs 37.5%, High 66.1% vs 67.3%. Once prior engagement is controlled for, the data shows no retention benefit, so it does not support the claim that the redesign improves retention.

The rates check out: control is 4671/61122 = 7.64% and treatment is 5022/60943 = 8.24%, a relative lift of about 7.8%. A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 3.9, so p is about 0.0001, consistent with p < 0.001. The split is also healthy. The 61,122 vs 60,943 user counts are within chance of 50/50 (z of about 0.5), so there is no sample ratio mismatch. The claim's numbers are supported by the data.

The headline numbers reproduce (4,803/10,782 = 44.5% vs 12,824/46,271 = 27.7%), but the gap is a composition effect. Adopters skew toward high prior engagement (43% of adopters vs 7% of non-adopters). Within each engagement tier, retention is about the same or slightly lower for adopters: Low 18.6% vs 18.2%, Medium 36.5% vs 37.2%, High 60.3% vs 62.3%. The data shows no retention benefit from guided setup after controlling for prior engagement, so the causal claim is not supported.

The headline numbers are arithmetically correct (adopters 4251/8847 = 48.1%, non-adopters 10808/44877 = 24.1%). But the gap is driven by prior engagement mix: adopters skew heavily toward High engagement users, who retain well regardless. Within each tier retention is nearly identical for adopters and non-adopters: Low 15.1% vs 14.3%, Medium 32.0% vs 32.2%, High 70.6% vs 70.0%. The data therefore shows confounding by prior engagement and gives no evidence that the redesign helps retention.

The headline rates match the data (B 2,866/12,699 = 22.6%, A 1,525/12,358 = 12.3%). But this is Simpson's paradox from a traffic-mix difference. Page B got mostly high-converting Referral traffic, and Page A got mostly low-converting Organic traffic. Within every channel Page A converts better: Referral 34.3% vs 31.1%, Email 13.2% vs 11.8%, Organic 7.8% vs 5.2%. The rollout was not randomized, so the aggregate gap reflects channel mix and not page quality. The data does not support calling Page B better, and if anything it points the other way.

The headline numbers check out: Page B is 2944/15535 = 18.9% and Page A is 2557/16618 = 15.4%. Because the rollout wasn't randomized, I checked whether channel mix explains the gap. It doesn't. Page B converts higher within every channel: Referral 33.9% vs 30.1%, Email 15.6% vs 10.9%, Organic 8.4% vs 5.8%. The channel mix is also nearly identical across pages, so there is no Simpson's-paradox effect. Unobserved differences such as device or campaign timing could still exist, but the consistent, channel-adjusted lift is enough to support standardizing on Page B.

The figures are correct: adopters retain 5212/8761 = 59.5% and non-adopters 10712/44963 = 23.8%. The gap is inflated by mix, since adopters skew toward High prior engagement (48% of adopters vs 8% of non-adopters). Within each tier adopters still retain better: Low 27.7% vs 13.8%, Medium 44.4% vs 32.1%, High 80.4% vs 70.5%. That is a much smaller gap than the headline 36 points. Users chose whether to adopt, and three coarse tiers cannot rule out remaining self-selection. The data is consistent with a positive effect but cannot show the redesign is causing better retention.

The headline figures reproduce: adopters 6189/10418 = 59.4%, non-adopters 14152/49834 = 28.4%. But adopters skew toward high prior engagement (48% of adopters vs 11% of non-adopters), so most of the 31-point gap is mix. Within each tier the gap is about 10-12 points: Low 28.7% vs 17.7%, Medium 48.6% vs 38.1%, High 78.3% vs 66.6%. The direction is consistent, but adoption was self-selected and prior-engagement tiers are coarse, so residual confounding remains. The data suggest a smaller association than claimed, not a demonstrated causal improvement from the redesign.

The overall rates match (A 2,970/12,543 = 23.7%, B 1,587/12,434 = 12.8%), but this is a Simpson's paradox driven by platform mix. Flow A got mostly high-converting Android traffic, and Flow B got mostly low-converting Web traffic. Within every platform Flow B converts better: Android 40.4% vs 33.3%, iOS 16.1% vs 12.9%, Web 7.4% vs 4.6%. The data also comes from a non-randomized rollout, so the aggregate comparison is confounded and does not show that Flow A is better.

The aggregate rates match the claim (B 21.1% vs A 12.9%), but the gap comes from regional mix. Flow B got mostly Mexico traffic, which converts well, and Flow A got mostly Japan traffic, which converts poorly. Within each region Flow A converts better: Mexico 30.1% vs 26.0%, US 17.1% vs 15.8%, Japan 7.5% vs 4.5%. This is Simpson's paradox, and the non-randomized rollout makes it worse. The data does not support making Flow B the default, and if anything it points the other way.

The headline figures reproduce: adopters retain 6156/10687 = 57.6% and non-adopters 12766/46366 = 27.5%. Adopters skew toward high prior engagement, so the raw gap overstates the effect. Within every engagement tier, though, adopters still retain better: Low 29.5% vs 18.1%, Medium 50.2% vs 37.0%, High 73.5% vs 61.1%, a gap of about 11-13 points each. The direction holds after controlling for prior engagement, which supports the claim, but the true effect is much smaller than 30 points. Self-selection within tiers remains a residual caveat.

The headline numbers check out: Flow A is 2963/14960 = 19.8% and Flow B is 2465/15250 = 16.2%. The rollout was not randomized and Flow A has more Android traffic, so I checked whether platform mix explains the gap. It does not. Flow A beats Flow B within every platform: Android 35.9% vs 33.4%, iOS 15.4% vs 13.5%, Web 7.2% vs 4.9%. The lead is consistent, so it is not a mix artifact. Unmeasured differences in traffic could still matter, but the platform-level check supports the claim.

The arithmetic checks out: 3/21 = 14.3%. Overall average: orders = 656+493+166+534+3+453+168 = 2473; sessions = 12737+7185+3282+10750+21+9020+2780 = 45775; 2473/45775 = 5.4%. Ratio 14.3/5.4 = 2.6x. But the claim of being the best-converting source 'by a wide margin' rests on only 21 sessions and 3 orders, which is far too small a sample to be reliable. Other sources: Email 493/7185 = 6.9%, Kestrel 168/2780 = 6.0%, so Lumen's rate is highest in point terms, but a 95% interval on 3/21 would span roughly 3% to 36%, overlapping with all other sources. The data cannot establish that Lumen is genuinely better.

Lumen converts at 484/2596 = 18.6%. Total orders are 4166 on 61,958 sessions, which is 6.7% overall, and 18.6/6.7 is about 2.8x. The other sources range from about 5.6% (Kestrel) to 6.7% (Bluebird), so Lumen is clearly the highest by a wide margin. The claim matches the data.

The headline rates check out: B is 3621/18933 = 19.1% and A is 2425/16075 = 15.1%. The rollout was not randomized and B's traffic has more Mexico (the highest-converting region), so I stratified by region. B still wins in every region: Mexico 30.3% vs 27.0%, US 17.4% vs 14.0%, Japan 7.4% vs 4.6%. The gap therefore isn't a regional mix artifact, and the within-region gaps are similar in size to the overall gap. Unobserved confounders such as channel could still exist, but the data supports B outperforming A and being made the default.

Harbor's 3 funded of 16 applications is 18.75%, so the 18.8% figure is arithmetically right. The sample is tiny, though: a single account either way moves the rate by about 6 points, and the confidence interval is very wide (roughly 4% to 46%). The 7.2% average also checks out: 4218 funded over 58,979 applications is about 7.15%. Even so, 16 applications cannot establish that Harbor is the best source 'by a wide margin'. Northwind, Paid search and the others have thousands of applications and rates of about 7.3-7.5%, and Harbor's rate is statistically indistinguishable from them.

The unweighted per-campaign averages check out (about 4.1% in October and 6.4% in November), but that rise comes from tiny campaigns with a few hundred to about 1,400 clicks. The three large campaigns (Partner Launch, Win-back, Spring Sale) each fell. Pooled across all clicks, conversion dropped from about 2.82% (3,767 / 133,386) to about 2.26% (2,987 / 132,184), and total conversions fell by 780. So the conclusion that overall campaign performance is up does not follow from the data.

The unweighted mean of per-campaign conversion rates is about 3.97% in October and 4.71% in November, matching the stated 4.0% and 4.7%. The click-weighted overall rate also rose, from 2.84% (3,785/133,386) to 3.43% (4,616/134,592). The three large campaigns (Partner Launch, Win-back, Spring Sale) all improved, so the gain is not an artifact of small campaigns. A couple of small campaigns dipped slightly, but overall performance is clearly up.

Lumen's 14.3% (2/14) rests on only 14 trials and 2 conversions, so the estimate is extremely noisy; a 95% interval would span roughly 2% to 43%, which easily includes the ~5.5-6% overall rate. Other sources have thousands of trials and rates around 4.5-6.1%, so the data cannot establish that Lumen is the best converter "by a wide margin." The arithmetic is right (2/14=14.3%; overall about 3,981 trials... roughly 5.6-5.8%, close to 5.5%), but the conclusion is not reliable given the sample size.

Harbor converts at 541/2388 = 22.65%, which rounds to 22.7%. The pooled average across all sources is 3597/46683 = 7.7%, and 22.65/7.7 is about 2.9x. The other sources range from about 6.3% (Organic search) to 7.4% (Paid search), so Harbor is clearly the best by a wide margin.

Lumen converts 354/1986 = 17.8%. The overall blended rate is 3126/50771 = 6.16%, or about 6.2%, and 17.8/6.2 is about 2.9x. The other sources range from 4.7% (Paid search) to 6.3% (Email), so Lumen is far ahead of every one. Its sample of 1,986 trials and 354 conversions is large enough that the gap is not noise. The 6.2% average includes Lumen itself, but that does not change the conclusion.

The unweighted average of per-campaign conversion rates does rise from about 4.7% to 7.0%. But the big three campaigns (Partner Launch, Retargeting, Brand Search), which carry over 90% of clicks, all declined. Pooled across all campaigns, conversions fell from 4,084 to 3,356 and the overall rate dropped from about 3.9% to 3.3%. The small campaigns' gains inflate the simple average, so the conclusion that overall performance is up does not follow.

The 24% figure checks out: 2025 signups fell from 23,808 (Aug 25–31) to 18,165 (Sep 1–7), a 23.7% drop. But the same two weeks in 2024, with no page launch, fell from 21,437 to 16,027, a 25.2% drop, including the same sharp Labor Day Monday dip. So the drop is a normal seasonal pattern, not an unusual one, and the timing does not implicate the new landing page.

Week of Apr 21–27, 2025 totals 23,965 signups and the launch week of Apr 28–May 4 totals 19,241, a drop of about 19.7%, so '20%' holds. The same weeks in 2024 show only about a 1% dip (21,812 to 21,587), so seasonality doesn't explain it and the drop is unusual. The decline begins sharply on Monday Apr 28, the launch day, so the timing does point at the new page, though the data alone can't rule out other changes that day.

The unweighted averages check out: about 3.9% in August and 6.0% in September. But that rise comes only from the small campaigns (roughly 500–1,400 clicks each). The three big campaigns, which carry most of the clicks, all fell: Creator Collab from 4.0% to 3.3%, Back to School from 3.0% to 2.5%, and Free Trial Push from 2.6% to 2.0%. Weighted by clicks, the overall conversion rate dropped from about 3.14% to 2.68%, and total conversions fell from 4,719 to 3,985. The claim that overall campaign performance is up therefore does not follow from the data.

Recomputing the unweighted mean of per-campaign conversion rates gives about 4.38% in August and 5.48% in September, matching the stated 4.4% and 5.5%. That simple mean is inflated by small campaigns like Webinar Series, Spring Sale and Creator Collab. Even so, the click-weighted pooled rate also rises, from about 3.89% (4,083/105,041) to 4.39% (4,565/104,046), and every campaign's rate went up. Total conversions also rose while clicks held roughly flat, so 'overall performance is up' holds.

The 24% figure is accurate: 2025 signups fell from 28,872 to 22,006 (-23.8%). But the drop is not unusual. The same two weeks in 2024, with no page launch, fell from 24,509 to 18,463 (-24.7%). The pattern is seasonal around the July 4 holiday week, including the Friday trough both years. The data contradicts the claim that the drop is unusual and attributable to the new page.

Recomputing the per-campaign rates gives an unweighted average of about 3.99% in August and 4.84% in September, which matches the claimed 4.0% and 4.8%. The improvement holds up beyond the simple average. Every one of the 10 campaigns raised its conversion rate. Pooled across all clicks, the rate rose from about 3.05% (4,589/150,463) to about 3.76% (5,647/150,279). Total clicks were roughly flat while total conversions rose about 23%, so overall performance is genuinely up.

The rate did jump from about 2.58% to 3.57% on 2025-07-14, but almost all of that comes from the denominator. Trial starts fell from roughly 79k to roughly 57k per day, while subscriptions stayed flat at about 2,000–2,100. The changelog shows a duplicate-trial filter was enabled the same day, which would remove trial starts without changing real conversions. The rise is therefore mostly a measurement artifact, not evidence that the annual plan offer improved conversion.

Over the 10 days before 2025-07-14, conversion averaged 2.51%, and over the 10 days from launch it averaged 3.32%, matching the claim. The jump from 2.51% on 07-13 to 3.40% on 07-14 (+0.89pp) is by far the largest day-over-day change in the window; other daily moves are about 0.1pp or less. The step coincides with the annual plan deploy, and no other change is logged that day. Trial starts are flat, so the gain comes from more subscriptions, not a smaller trial base.

Pre-launch averages around 3.6% and post-launch around 5.08%, so the arithmetic holds. But trials fell about 30% (roughly 52-53k down to about 37k) on 2025-06-02 while paid conversions stayed flat at about 1.8-2.0k. The changelog shows a spam-signup filter went live the same day. The filter shrank the denominator by removing junk trials, so the rate jump does not show that the pricing page drove more paid conversions. Since absolute conversions did not rise, crediting the pricing page is not supported.

The 24% figure is accurate: signups went from 24,104 in the week of May 19, 2025 to 18,425 in the week of May 26. But the same weeks in 2024, before the new page existed, show a similar drop of about 26% (20,846 to 15,415), including a Memorial Day Monday dip (1,490 vs. 1,769 this year). The drop is a normal seasonal pattern rather than an unusual one, so the timing does not point to the new page.

Week of Apr 21–27, 2025 totals 29,003 signups and the week of Apr 28–May 4 totals 24,358, a 16.0% drop, so the figure is accurate. The same weeks last year were flat (24,274 to 24,402, +0.5%), so this is not a recurring seasonal dip. The decline also starts exactly on launch Monday (3,719 vs 4,319 the prior Monday). The data supports both the size and the unusualness of the drop, and the timing is consistent with the new page as the cause.

The 2025 week after launch (Oct 20–26) totals 19,813 signups against 24,106 the week before, a 17.8% drop, which matches the claimed 18%. The same two weeks in 2024 actually rose about 1.4%, so this is not a seasonal pattern and the drop is genuinely unusual. The decline starts on Monday Oct 20 itself (3,047 vs 3,611 the prior Monday) and holds every day after, which fits the launch timing.

The 2025-10 cohort is only partially matured. Data was pulled 2025-11-12, so only 2,309 of 5,555 signups (those from roughly Oct 1–13) have reached day 30. That early-October subset may not represent the full month, and the cohort's final rate could differ substantially. The 32.9% figure is computed correctly for that subset, but it is not a like-for-like comparison with the fully matured earlier cohorts, which average about 21.8%. The data cannot yet establish that the newest users retain better.

The data pull on 2025-12-10 is more than 30 days after every October signup, so the full 2025-10 cohort is measurable (5,983 of 5,983 users). Its day-30 retention is 2016/5983 = 33.7%. The pooled May–September figure is 4264/19238 ≈ 22.2%, and each of those months sits between 20.6% and 23.2%, so the jump is real and not an artifact of an incomplete cohort. One caveat: the table counts all signups, not specifically trial users, but this doesn't change the retention comparison.

The conversion rate did rise from about 2.81% to 3.86%, but the rise came from a smaller denominator, not more subscriptions. Trial starts fell from roughly 71k to roughly 50k per day while subscriptions stayed flat at about 1.9–2.0k. A duplicate-trial filter was enabled on the same day (2025-09-20), which most plausibly explains the drop in counted trials. The jump therefore looks like a measurement artifact, and the data does not show that autoplay previews improved conversion.

Data was pulled 2025-09-13, so only 1,360 of 3,056 August signups (those from roughly Aug 1–14) have reached day 30. That makes the August cohort a partial, early-month subset, and early-month signups may differ systematically from the full cohort. The 31.5% figure is computed correctly but cannot yet be compared like-for-like with the earlier fully matured cohorts (~22%). The data cannot establish whether newest customers are really retaining better.

Average conversion over the 10 days before 2025-06-02 is 3.62%, and over the 10 days from launch it is 4.88%, which matches the claim. The 2025-06-01→06-02 jump (3.73%→4.90%, about +1.2 points) is by far the largest day-over-day change in the data, so 'biggest single-day improvement' holds within this window. Trials stayed flat while paid conversions rose, so this is not a denominator artifact. The only change logged on 06-02 is the pricing page itself.

With the pull on 2025-10-10, every August signup has had at least 30 days elapsed (users_with_30_days_elapsed equals signups), so the cohort is complete and not censored. The 2025-08 rate is 1470/4524 = 32.5%. The pooled earlier cohorts come to 4418/20260 = 21.8%, and each earlier month sits between 20.9% and 22.7%. The figures match the claim, and the jump is well outside the earlier range.

The drop in iOS lesson_started_events is real in the data: about 8.2% of visits before 2025-04-01 and about 0.5% after. But the conclusion that learners stopped starting lessons and that revenue is being lost does not follow. iOS enrollments, which come from the production database, held steady at roughly 2,100–2,300 per day. iOS visits, from server logs, were also flat. Only the client-side SDK metric collapsed, which points to an analytics instrumentation or SDK break on iOS rather than a change in learner behavior or revenue.

Pre-April iOS lesson starts average about 5,860 per day on roughly 52,600 visits (≈11.1%). From 2025-04-01 they fall to about 443 per day on roughly 52,300 visits (≈0.85%), matching the claimed figures. This could in principle be a client-side SDK tracking failure, but iOS enrollments come from the separate production database and fall in step, from about 1,920 to about 140 per day. iOS visits and Web/Android metrics stay flat, so the collapse is real behavior specific to iOS and plausibly hits revenue.

The before/after numbers check out. The 10 days before 2025-09-20 average about 2.80%, and the 10 days from 2025-09-20 average about 3.69%. The step change lines up exactly with the autoplay deploy, and trial starts stay flat. However, the claim also says this is 'the biggest single-day improvement we've seen'. The ratio drop is real: Web title-play events fell from about 11.8% to about 1.0% of trial starts starting 2025-07-25. But Web trial starts (server logs) and Web subscriptions (production DB) held steady or rose slightly after that date. Subscriptions went from roughly 1013–1075/day to 1090–1150/day, so there is no sign of lost revenue. Title-play events come from the client-side SDK, so a sudden ~92% drop on one platform with healthy downstream conversions looks more like a tracking or instrumentation break than users actually stopping playing. The data does not support the claim that Web users stopped playing or that revenue is being lost.

The table gives 2025-07 day-30 retention as 1363/4275 = 31.9%. Pooling the February–June cohorts gives 5589/22988 ≈ 24.3%, and each of those months falls between 23% and 26%. The data was pulled on 2025-09-09, so even late-July signups had more than 30 days elapsed and the July figure is fully observed. The 'trial users' wording loosely refers to the signup cohort, but the numbers support a clear jump in retention for the newest cohort.

The arithmetic holds: July's 624/2073 is 30.1%, and February–June average about 24.4%. But only 2,073 of July's 5,913 signups (about 35%) have reached day 30 by the 2025-08-11 pull, so the figure covers early-July signups only. Users who joined at the start of the month may differ systematically from the full cohort (for example through promotions or timing effects), so this data cannot establish whether the whole July cohort, or new trial users generally, retain better.

The headline numbers are right: blended conversion went from 7,582/160,349 (4.7%) to 6,426/162,503 (4.0%). The explanation does not follow, though. Within each channel, rates held roughly flat or rose: Email 6.8%→7.0%, Organic search 4.5%→4.5%, Paid social 3.0%→3.1%, Paid search 0.9%→0.9%. The decline comes from mix shift, as low-converting Paid search trials jumped from about 12k to 45k while the other channels shrank. So visitors are not 'just converting less'; the place to look is the Paid search volume change, not a broad funnel problem.

Aggregate conversion went from 7,989/166,408 (4.80%) to 6,168/158,352 (3.90%), matching the stated figures. Channel mix barely changed between the two weeks, and every channel's rate dropped: Email 6.8%→5.7%, Organic 4.7%→3.6%, Paid social 3.0%→2.4%, Paid search 0.9%→0.6%. Because the drop is broad-based rather than a mix shift, the claim that trial users are simply converting less holds.

Web add-to-cart events did collapse from roughly 3,500/day (~14.9% of sessions) to about 220/day (~0.9%) starting 2025-04-15. However, Web orders, which come from the production database, held steady at about 480–570/day, the same as before. Web sessions were also unchanged. Since orders now far exceed add-to-cart events, the drop looks like a client-side analytics SDK tracking break rather than customers having trouble. The data contradicts the claim that we're losing orders.

The figures check out. Pooled over each week, Web title-play rate was 32,501/218,547 = 14.9% for Jul 18–24, then 2,412/219,735 = 1.1% from Jul 25 onward. Trial starts held steady and the other platforms show no change. Title plays come from the client SDK, so the drop alone could be a tracking break. However, Web subscriptions, recorded independently in the production database, fell by the same ~90% on the same day (about 1,170/day to about 130/day). That makes a real Web breakage with revenue impact the consistent reading.

Web add-to-cart fell from about 14.2% of app sessions (45,019/316,640) in Apr 8–14 to about 1.0% (3,263/316,798) from Apr 15 on, while Web sessions held steady. Web orders, which come from the production database rather than the client-side SDK, dropped about 90% at the same time (~1,450/day to ~155/day). That rules out a tracking-only artifact and backs the conclusion that real orders are being lost. iOS and Android show no change, so the problem is specific to Web.

The topline figures check out: 6,965/172,465 is 4.04% and 5,780/169,704 is 3.41%. But within each channel conversion held steady or improved: Paid social 5.24%→5.22%, Paid search 4.47%→4.64%, Referral 2.79%→2.85%, Email 1.15%→1.24%. The drop comes from channel mix. Totals check out: 6,927/171,687 = 4.03% the first week and 5,689/168,430 = 3.38% the second. The drop is not a channel-mix artifact. Channel shares of sessions barely changed, and conversion fell within every channel: Paid social 5.17%→4.25%, Paid search 4.51%→3.93%, Referral 2.82%→2.28%, Email 1.18%→0.94%. So users really are converting worse, which justifies investigating the funnel. The data cannot confirm a funnel break as the cause; seasonality or pricing could also explain it.

The overall rate does fall from about 4.08% to 3.34% (7,717/189,325 vs 6,249/187,361). However, per-channel rates are nearly flat: Paid search, Referral and Organic each tick up slightly, and Paid social slips only from 6.3% to 6.1%. The aggregate drop comes mainly from a mix shift, with Organic search, the lowest-converting channel at about 1.3%, nearly tripling from 21.9k to 64.1k applications while higher-converting channels shrank. So the data does not show a broken funnel, and the place to look is the traffic mix (why Organic surged and paid volume fell).

Twenty countries were tested separately, and Australia is the only one with p < 0.05. At an alpha of 0.05, about one false positive is expected across 20 tests, and a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.0025 makes p = 0.019 non-significant. The overall result is flat, so this looks like a subgroup picked after the fact rather than a real effect. A country-specific launch would need a pre-registered replication first.

Overall rate goes from 7,791/189,960 = 4.10% to 6,098/185,117 = 3.29%, matching the claim. Channel mix barely shifted, and every channel's rate fell by a similar share (about 20–25%). Paid social went 6.25%→4.98%, paid search 3.70%→3.01%, referral 2.71%→2.16% and organic 1.26%→0.94%. So this is a real, broad conversion decline rather than a mix effect, which fits a funnel-wide issue worth investigating. One caveat: the newer week may have had less time for applications to reach funded status.

Argentina is the only one of 20 countries with p < 0.05, and the result is reported without any multiple-comparisons correction. With 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, roughly one false positive is expected by chance. A Bonferroni threshold would be 0.0025, and p = 0.028 is far from that. The lifts across countries scatter in both directions around zero, which fits noise rather than a real effect localized to Argentina. The data does not justify an Argentina-only launch; at most it justifies a confirmatory test in Argentina.

France is the only one of 20 country-level tests to reach p < 0.05, and the overall result is flat. With 20 comparisons, about one false positive at p ≈ 0.03 is expected by chance. After a multiple-comparison correction (Bonferroni threshold ≈ 0.0025), France's p = 0.031 is not significant. The data gives no reliable evidence of a France-specific effect, so it does not justify launching there. A pre-registered confirmation test in France would be needed.

Turkey's numbers check out: 185/2853 (6.48%) vs 256/2835 (9.03%) is a +39.3% lift, and a two-proportion z-test gives z≈3.6, p≈0.0003. Since 20 countries were tested, multiple comparisons are a concern, but p=0.0003 stays below the Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/20=0.0025. Pooled conversions are flat globally (5386 vs 5326 on similar user counts), consistent with 'didn't move the global number'. The negative results in Canada, Brazil and Singapore do not survive correction, so the Turkey effect stands out as robust and the data support the claim.

Netherlands goes from 258/4316 (5.98%) to 385/4489 (8.58%), a +43.5% relative lift with z ≈ 4.7 (p ≈ 3e-6). Twenty countries were tested, so this could be a multiple-comparisons artifact. But the result survives a Bonferroni correction (threshold 0.05/20 = 0.0025) by a wide margin, so it is very unlikely to be chance. The other countries show small, non-significant, mixed effects, which fits a flat global result. A confirmatory Netherlands test would still be prudent, but the data back the claim as stated.

South Africa converts at 7.46% in control (250/3350) and 10.61% in treatment (349/3288), a 42.2% relative lift. A two-proportion test gives z ≈ 4.9 (p ≈ 1e-6). That is far below a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/20 = 0.0025, so the result survives correction for testing 20 countries post hoc. The other countries show small, non-significant mixed effects, consistent with a flat overall result. The data support the South Africa win and a targeted launch there.

The pooled lift is driven by a novelty effect that fades. In week 1, treatment converted at about 9.97% versus 8.82% for control, roughly a +13% lift. By week 3, treatment trailed control (about 8.94% vs 9.17%), and in week 4 the two arms were essentially equal (about 9.03% vs 9.01%). The 28-day average therefore overstates the ongoing effect, and forecasting a +3.4% lift going forward does not follow from the data.

The pooled lift is driven by a novelty spike that fades. Treatment ran about 18–21% above control on days 1–2 (12.8% vs ~10.7%), but by day 7 the two arms are roughly equal and alternate day to day. Over days 15–28 the arms convert at about 11.0% (control) vs 11.2% (treatment), roughly +1.4% relative, which is likely within noise. The 28-day average overstates the steady-state effect, so forecasting +3.5% going forward does not follow from the data.

The overall lift is driven almost entirely by the first week. In days 1–7 treatment converts about 12.4% vs about 11.2% for control, roughly a +10% relative lift. From day 8 onward the arms are essentially equal (e.g., day 8: 11.69% vs 11.69%; day 9: 11.83% vs 11.34%), with near-zero lift through day 28. This pattern looks like a novelty effect that decays, so the 4-week average of +3.2% overstates the steady-state effect and does not support planning on a durable +3.2% lift.

The +$13,981 treatment revenue gap comes entirely from two outlier orders ($12,735 and $3,995, totalling $16,730). Without them, treatment revenue (~$107,120) falls below control's $109,868. Purchasers are essentially identical (1,985 vs 1,986), and treatment's median and p95 order values are slightly lower. The lift reflects two extreme orders, not a reliable effect of one-click checkout, so the claim does not follow from the data.

The figures check out: $122,832.94 / 41,018 = $2.995 and $106,310.84 / 41,018 = $2.592, a +15.5% lift. The lift comes from broad gains rather than outliers: purchasers rose from 1,972 to 2,145 (+8.8%, roughly z≈2.8), and median order value also rose ($43.31 to $44.80). The largest orders are evenly split between arms (4 each) and of similar size, so no whale order drives the result. A rough variance estimate puts the revenue-per-user difference at about 4 standard errors, so the claim holds.

Pooled over 28 days, control converts at 26,478/296,361 (8.93%) and treatment at 28,303/296,943 (9.53%). That is a +6.7% relative lift with z ≈ 8, so p < 0.001 holds. Weekly lifts are about 7.8%, 7.1%, 4.0% and 7.7%, which is noisy but shows no sustained decay. A novelty effect is therefore not evident, and a +6.7% forecast is reasonable.

The arithmetic is correct, but the lift comes almost entirely from two treatment orders ($11,551.61 and $4,060.64, about $15,612 combined), set against a total revenue gap of about $16,582. Without those two orders treatment leads by only about $970, roughly 0.7%. Purchasers rise just 1.5% and median order value is actually lower in treatment. The 11.6% per-user lift is outlier-driven and does not justify a rollout.

Summing the table gives control at 32,069/294,353 (10.89%) and treatment at 34,910/294,621 (11.85%). That is a +8.8% relative lift with z ≈ 11, consistent with p < 0.001. Weekly lifts run about 9.7%, 8.1%, 9.3% and 8.0%, with no clear novelty decay, so using +8.8% for the forecast is reasonable.

The figures check out: 165,900.95/52,583 = $3.155 and 134,655.91/52,583 = $2.561, a 23.2% lift. The gain does not depend on outliers. It comes from more purchasers (2,720 vs 2,393, about +13.7%, z≈4.8 on conversion) and a higher median order value ($47.64 vs $44.11). The largest single order is actually in control. Rollout is a judgement call, but the data supports the revenue readout as stated.

Pooled over 28 days, control converts at about 11.32% (33,664/297,481) and treatment at about 12.02% (35,871/298,326). That is a +6.3% relative lift with z ≈ 8, consistent with p < 0.001. Weekly lifts are roughly +5.4%, +7.7%, +4.2% and +7.7%, so there is no decaying novelty pattern and the effect holds through week 4. That makes planning on a sustained lift of about this size reasonable, though behaviour beyond the test window can't be directly verified.

The $15,616 revenue gap between arms is almost entirely three treatment orders ($7,597.75, $4,242.01 and $3,659.78, about $15,500 combined). Without them, treatment revenue is about $137,647 against control's $137,531, essentially identical. Treatment also had slightly fewer purchasers (2,379 vs 2,399) and a lower p95 order value, so there is no broad-based lift. The +11.3% comes from a few outliers, not a reliable effect of one-click checkout, so the shipping conclusion does not follow.

The figures are accurate: 1036/11754 = 8.81%, 1118/11695 = 9.56%, and p = 0.048 on day 5. The figures check out: $134,677.85/42,742 = $3.151 and $153,503.85/42,742 = $3.591, a 14.0% lift. The seven largest orders are all in treatment, but even removing them entirely (about $3.8K) leaves treatment roughly $15K ahead of the $18.8K total gap, so outliers do not drive the result. The lift comes from higher conversion: 6.01% vs 5.43% (z ≈ 3.6), with a similar median order value. The revenue gain looks robust.

The table runs the full planned 28 days, and the context says results were analyzed once at the end, so there is no early-stopping concern. Day 28 gives control 5741/62251 = 9.22% and treatment 6368/62030 = 10.27%. The p-value is reported as 0.0, and my own check gives z ≈ 6.2, consistent with p < 0.001. The figures check out: 574/7598 = 7.55% vs 652/7461 = 8.74%, with p = 0.0079 on day 3. However, the test was planned for 28 days and stopped the first day the daily p-value crossed 0.05, after peeking on days 1–3. Three days also may not capture weekly cycles or novelty effects. The decision to ship does not follow from this data without a sequential-testing correction or running the planned duration.

The 4.2-point figure checks out: the 10 lowest September scorers, all coached, averaged +4.21 in October. But the history table shows the bottom 10 gained 6.4 to 9.0 points per month before coaching existed, which is consistent with regression to the mean. A 4.2-point gain is below that no-coaching baseline, so it is not evidence the program pays off.

The bottom 10 September scorers (all of them coached) rose by an average of about 18.35 points, which matches the claimed 18.4. Some of this is regression to the mean: before the program, the bottom 10 typically rebounded by 7.2–8.6 points a month. Even so, October's gain is more than double that baseline, leaving roughly 10 points of excess improvement. That supports the program having an effect, though the true effect is closer to 10 points than 18.4.

On day 28, control converted 5143/60180 users (8.55%) and treatment converted 5549/59690 users (9.30%). The final p-value is about 0; recomputing gives z ≈ 4.5, so p < 0.001. The coached stores' average change does come to about +9.1 (sum of changes 91.3 / 10). The arithmetic checks out: 3760/65465 = 5.74%, 4576/71829 = 6.37%, about a +10.9% relative lift. However, the configured split was 50/50, and treatment has 71,829 users against control's 65,465. Recomputing from the table gives 5.87% for control (4021/68558) and 6.22% for treatment (4276/68736), a relative lift of about +6.1%. The conversion rates are computed correctly: 3768/50322 = 7.49% and 4579/57326 = 7.99%. Control converts at 4040/53972 = 7.49% and treatment at 4312/53676 = 8.03%, a +7.3% relative lift. A two-proportion z-test gives z ≈ 3.36, so p ≈ 0.0008, which is below 0.001. The 16.9-point figure checks out, and the 10 coached stores are indeed the 10 lowest April scorers. But because they were picked for being lowest, some rebound is expected anyway. Before coaching existed, the bottom 10 rose 2.3–7.7 points a month, so the raw 16.9 overstates the coaching effect. With no comparable uncoached low-scoring group, the true effect can't be isolated. Nothing here shows coaching would help higher-scoring stores either, so 'coaching works, roll it out to everyone' does not follow.

The conversion rates check out: 4310/57523 = 7.49% and 5217/64542 = 8.08%. However, the split is badly off a configured 50/50: 57,523 vs 64,542 users (47.1% vs 52.9%). Control converts at 4671/61122 = 7.64% and treatment at 5022/60943 = 8.24%, a +7.8% relative lift, matching the claim. A two-proportion z-test gives z ≈ 3.9 (p ≈ 0.0001), so p < 0.001 holds. The aggregate figures check out: adopters retain at 4947/10369 = 47.7% and non-adopters at 14056/49883 = 28.2%. Within every prior-engagement tier, though, adopters retain about the same or slightly worse: Low 17.4% vs 17.5%, Medium 36.9% vs 37.5%, High 66.1% vs 67.3%. The overall gap comes from adopters being disproportionately high-engagement users (Simpson's paradox), so the data does not show the redesign improving retention.

The pooled figures are arithmetically correct: 4251/8847 = 48.1% for adopters and 10808/44877 = 24.1% for non-adopters. The gap comes from composition, though, because adopters are concentrated in the High prior-engagement tier. Within each tier retention is nearly identical for adopters and non-adopters: Low 15.1% vs 14.3%, Medium 32.0% vs 32.2%, High 70.6% vs 70.0%. Once prior engagement is accounted for, the data shows no meaningful retention benefit, so the conclusion that the redesign is helping retention does not follow.

The pooled figures are correct (6189/10418 = 59.4% vs 14152/49834 = 28.4%), but adopters skew heavily toward high prior engagement, and that tier retains far better regardless of feature use. Within each tier the gap shrinks to about 10–12 points: Low 28.7% vs 17.7%, Medium 48.6% vs 38.1%, High 78.3% vs 66.6%. So most of the 31-point headline gap reflects who chose to adopt, not the page itself. Even the remaining within-tier gap comes from self-selected, observational data and does not establish that the redesign causes better retention.

The figures are arithmetically correct: 5212/8761 = 59.5% for adopters and 10712/44963 = 23.8% for non-adopters. But the comparison is confounded by prior engagement.
